meaning: The MBTA's operating day. Trains running after midnight still count toward the day they started.

Weekday, Saturday, Sunday or holiday. Holidays (listed in board_data.json meta.holidays) are their own type because the MBTA runs a weekend schedule on most of them, so weekday figures leave them out.

Every service date in the window: weekdays, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays. The late-trip, time-over-schedule and long-gap headline numbers are over all days; train time over schedule, gate entries and rider time lost are for an average weekday (train time over schedule and rider time lost also give the all-days average).
How long the published schedule gives a train to get from one stop to the next.
Actual time between stops minus scheduled time. Positive means slower than the schedule.

A train run whose actual time between its first and last compared stops was more than 5 minutes longer than scheduled. The same 5-minute rule applies on every line, so long lines are more exposed to it.
For one train run, the sum of (actual minus scheduled) time over its compared stop-to-stop segments. Averaged per trip, not per stop.
Total excess time divided by total scheduled run time. Compares lines of different length on an equal footing.
The gap between one train leaving a station and the next train on the same line leaving it.
A wait more than 1.5 times the scheduled gap, e.g. 12+ minutes when trains are due every 8.
A train leaving a station less than half the scheduled gap after the train before it.
Share of gaps between half and 1.5 times the scheduled gap.
Fare-gate entries at a station, from MBTA's published counts. Each entry is counted once, on one line. One person can make several entries a day, so entries are not riders.
MBTA time-of-day bands from its Service Delivery Policy, e.g. AM Peak 7:00-8:59.

For each station, line and time of day: average gated entries times the share of train departures that came after a long gap, summed. An estimate of how many entries happen during long gaps, not a head count of people who waited.

An estimate, not a measurement: it is based on people entering stations through fare gates and assumes riders arrive at random times. In rider-seconds: for each station, line, time of day and day, gate entries times (extra expected wait + extra run time on the next segment). Expected wait for someone arriving at a random time is the sum of squared gaps divided by twice the sum of gaps (the standard headway-based formula), so long gaps count for more. Not clamped at zero: trains that ran better than scheduled offset those that ran worse. Shown without and with the gaps over 1 hour. The share of total rider time lost counts wait and ride together. The headline is an average weekday; train time over schedule is the measured headline.
The stretch of track between two consecutive stations on a line, in one direction. Branches that share track share segments.
How much extra time to plan for a segment so you are on time 9 times out of 10: the 90th percentile run time minus the median run time. Buffer index is that divided by the median.

The last 14 service dates compared with the 28 before them. Flagged only with at least 300 train runs or departures in the recent window and 600 in the prior one (about 21 a day), when excess time rose by at least 5 s and by at least 5 s more than the typical (median) change. The recent and prior values and the deltas behind the flag are in the files for every row.

For segments with at least 20 days of 20+ train runs: bias is the median daily average net excess, variability is the spread (interquartile range) of those daily values. 'Schedule' when |bias| is at least twice the spread (consistently off: the scheduled time is wrong), 'service' when the spread is at least twice |bias| (delivery varies day to day), otherwise 'mixed'.

Times are stored in exact seconds and shown with their two largest units: 55 s, 1 min 29 s, 1 h 3 min, 2 days 4 h, 3 months 10 days, 1 year 2 months. 1 month = 30 days and 1 year = 365 days. What is cut below the second unit is rounded to the nearest second unit (halves up) and carried, so 119 s stays 1 min 59 s but 3750 s (1 h 2 min 30 s) is 1 h 3 min and 86380 s (23 h 59 min 40 s) is 1 day. A zero second unit is dropped.

Measured from recorded train runs, not estimated: for every run between two stops, the actual time minus the scheduled time, added up over a day. Positive counts late time only (a run 30 s early counts as 0); net lets early runs offset late ones. Runs over 30 minutes are included and also shown on their own. The headline is an average weekday; it is also given per run.

Positive excess is max(actual - scheduled, 0) per run: late time only. Net excess is actual - scheduled, so faster-than-scheduled runs count against slower ones. Both are given everywhere, in exact seconds.

Time a train spends on the platform at a line or branch terminal before it leaves, from the recorded arrival and departure there. It is shown on its own and not counted as train delay. Holding outside a terminal before pulling in cannot be separated (the data has no timestamp for it), so it stays in the run time of segments that end at a terminal.

Gaps of more than an hour between trains at a platform, usually a suspension with shuttle buses. They are kept in their own columns. Each is checked against the recorded departures: where trains were recorded leaving the platform inside the gap, the wait is split at those departures; a gap that starts on an earlier service date would run through the overnight break and is not counted as a wait.

Segments are ranked by measured train delay: positive excess seconds over weekday train runs, per average weekday. Rider numbers on a segment are only the people entering its start station, and they are not used in the rank.
The most recent service date with recorded data (board_data.json meta.service_date). The front of the board answers for that one day; the 90-day figures are a second view.

For a measure on one day: the median (and mean) of the same measure on the most recent 28 earlier service dates of the same day type that had data for that line, station or segment. The difference is the day's value minus the typical value. Early in the window fewer than 28 earlier days exist; the number used is given as typical_days.

An hour on the heatmap is worse than usual when its value is above the 75th percentile of the same hour on the typical days, better than usual when below the 25th percentile, and about usual in between. Hours with fewer than 20 trips, runs or departures, or fewer than 4 typical days, are not rated.

Hour of the day in Boston time, counted from midnight at the start of the service date, so 24 to 27 are trains running after midnight. Trips count in the hour they start; runs in the hour they arrive; gaps in the hour of the departure.
How many trips (or stop-to-stop runs) finished in each 1-minute band of time over or under schedule. Bands below -15 minutes and at 30 minutes or more are combined into one open band at each end.
A line's positive train time over schedule divided by the total over all subway lines, for one day, all weekdays or all days. The shares add up to 1.
